Month-long user: feels like the next step after tab complete -> prompts -> agents, and interacting with agents this way felt natural. The biggest advantage is that each bot owns its own routines, context and domain, and bots can communicate with each other. Keeping bots separated by domain gives better results as they build their own skills.
Because each bot has its own computer, async work 'actually works.' The user hasn't had to juggle git worktrees for the last month.
Biggest downside is token expenditure. The user says they used more tokens in one month than in the prior 5 years combined, because always-on perpetual agents use a LOT of tokens.

Coolest use: one bot contacted ~40 fabric suppliers in Vietnam, negotiated prices, locked one in and got samples made for custom swag. It worked with a 'prototyper' bot that generated a pattern from the user's logo and sent it to the supplier as a .ai file.

Has done something similar with OpenClaw using multiple Telegram bots with different system prompts. That was non-trivial, and bot-to-bot communication never worked. Grok Bot simplifies this setup about as far as possible and is 'a pretty slick experience.'
Commenter says it appears preferable to Claude Code desktop, though unsure it's the end-all.
Pricing is $120/$200 per month per employee. Commenter doubts many companies are comfortable giving SpaceXAI access to all their files and data, and thinks it likely won't fly outside America.

Compared to the remote Claude instances they already use daily, it seems to have no safeguards. It targets less technical users but asks them to upload every login to Elon's servers, which the commenter calls insane.
The scariest part is the first landing-page video, where the bot just grabs your credentials from the browser and takes over. The commenter worries many people will hand X all their data and creds.
Commenter says Musk's personal brand is so poisonous that they would never let him near their data. They wonder whether big businesses will avoid SpaceXAI tools for the same reason.

Commenter sees no reason to use it at a company, since it means betting on Grok having the best models. An open-source agent lets you use any model, and coding-agent users already moved off Claude Code to open-source agents and models to cut costs.

Comparison: a commenter runs a self-built async agent (Codex + systemd + email) on a $20/month ChatGPT Plus subscription. It triaged and resolved 25+ bugs while they were on holiday. They grant Grok Bot sounds more sophisticated, but they haven't needed more than one bot because they can't saturate even one.

Seen as a middle ground between ChatGPT/Claude work modes and OpenClaw/Hermes, essentially standard chat plus seamless memory and skill creation. The humanization of the agents is called cute and sensible UX-wise.
Commenter notes everyone is shipping in-house agent solutions and they all seem 'kinda the same.'
